card.body: Allicin carries the official GHS signal word "Warning". Its hazard statements: causes skin irritation, causes serious eye irritation, and may cause respiratory irritation.

card.title: Discovered in Japan in the 1940s
card.body: In 1944, Chester J. Cavallito and John Hays Bailey first isolated and studied allicin in the laboratory. It was discovered during efforts to create thiamine derivatives in Japan. Allicin became a model for developing other thiamine disulfides such as sulbutiamine, fursultiamine, and benfothiamine.

card.title: Official signal word: Danger
card.body: Artemisinin carries the official GHS signal word "Danger". Its hazard statements: heating may cause a fire, very toxic to aquatic life, and very toxic to aquatic life with long lasting effects.

card.title: From ancient herb to antimalarial discovery
card.body: In 1596, Li Shizhen recommended tea made from sweet wormwood to treat malaria symptoms in his Compendium of Materia Medica. In 1967, a secret military program called 'Project 523' was launched by the People's Liberation Army under Mao Zedong's order to find a malaria treatment. In 1972, Tu Youyou discovered artemisinin in the leaves of Artemisia annua, inspired by a 340 CE herbal text by Ge Hong.

card.title: In sweet wormwood and malaria treatment
card.body: Artemisinin is found in Artemisia annua, also known as sweet wormwood, sweet annie, sweet sagewort, and annual wormwood. It is used in antimalarial drugs, especially for Plasmodium falciparum malaria, and appears in Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) as standard treatment worldwide. It has also been used in traditional medicine for malaria, cancer, viral and bacterial infections, and some cardiovasculreviear diseases.

card.title: Lind's citrus experiment
card.body: In May 1747, James Lind, a ship's surgeon in the Royal Navy, conducted one of the first controlled experiments by giving some crew members oranges and lemons while others received cider, vinegar, sulfuric acid, or seawater. He found citrus fruits prevented scurvy. Lind published his findings in 1753 in his Treatise on the Scurvy.

card.title: Discovery of batrachotoxin in frogs
card.body: In 1963, Fritz Märki and Bernhard Witkop isolated the toxic alkaloid fraction from the black-legged poison dart frog at the National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases in Bethesda, Maryland. They identified four major toxic steroidal alkaloids, including batrachotoxin, homobatrachotoxin, pseudobatrachotoxin, and batrachotoxinin A. The process was challenging due to the toxin's potency and scarcity.

The toxin forms in blisters when frogs are roasted or held over fire, and can cause instant nerve paralysis in monkeys and birds.

card.title: In your blue jeans and plants
card.body: Indigo is found in the leaves of Indigofera tinctoria plants, where it naturally forms a blue pigment. Today, most indigo is synthetic and used in denim production, with a pair of jeans requiring 3–12 grams of dye. It's also used in small amounts for wool and silk dyeing.

card.title: Indigo's ancient roots in India
card.body: The oldest known indigo-dyed fabric dates to 6,000 years ago and was found in Huaca Prieta, Peru. The Indigofera tinctoria species was domesticated in India, which became the earliest major center for its production and processing. India was also the source of indigo used by the Greeks and Romans, who valued it as a luxury product.

card.title: Indigo turns soluble with bacteria's hydrogen
card.body: In Japan, indigo was dissolved using thermophilic, anaerobic bacteria that generate hydrogen. This hydrogen converts insoluble indigo into soluble indigo white. The process relies on bacterial metabolism, not chemical reagents. Cloth was then decorated using shibori, kasuri, katazome, and tsutsugaki techniques.

card.body: Limonene is the main fragrance in citrus fruit peels, especially lemons and oranges. It appears in food manufacturing as a flavoring agent and in medicines to mask bitter tastes. You’ll also find it in personal care products like aftershave and bath items, and in cleaning products such as hand cleansers for its lemony scent and oil-dissolving power.

card.title: From opium to morphine in 1804
card.body: In December 1804, German pharmacist Friedrich Sertürner extracted morphine from the opium poppy plant in Paderborn. He noticed the compound induced drowsiness in rats and stray dogs and reported his findings in 1805. Sertürner named it morphium after the Greek god of dreams, Morpheus, due to its sleep-inducing effect.

card.title: From tobacco to isolation
card.body: In 1828, Wilhelm Heinrich Posselt and Karl Ludwig Reimann isolated nicotine from the tobacco plant in Germany, believing it was a poison. They identified its empirical formula in 1843 by Melsens, and its structure was discovered in 1893 by Adolf Pinner and Richard Wolffenstein. Nicotine was first synthesized in 1904 by Amé Pictet and A. Rotschy.

He named it 'pyroglycerin' and warned against its use as an explosive. The compound was later adopted by Alfred Nobel for commercial use after a deadly explosion in 1864.

card.title: In medicine and in dynamite
card.body: Nitroglycerin is prescribed for angina pectoris and as an antihypertensive, where it dilates veins to reduce heart preload. It is also found in formulations like Isordil and Imdur, converted to nitric oxide in the body. Historically, Alfred Nobel mixed it with diatomaceous earth to create dynamite, supplied as sticks wrapped in greased paper, used in tunneling, mining, and demolition.

card.title: From Quechua bark to Jesuit testing
card.body: The Quechua Indians of Peru, Bolivia, and Ecuador used ground cinchona bark mixed with sweetened water to treat shivering. Spanish Jesuit missionaries, including Agostino Salumbrino, observed this practice and sent cinchona bark to Rome for testing in the 17th century. Salumbrino, an apothecary in Lima, was the first to send a sample to Rome to evaluate its effect on malaria-induced shivering.

Historic records suggest its use in Europe as early as 1640 to kill animals and humans.

The compound was sucralose, patented by Tate & Lyle in 1976.

card.title: TTX is deadlier than cyanide, even by mouth
card.body: Tetrodotoxin is extremely toxic. Its oral LD50 for mice is 334 μg per kg, which is less than that of potassium cyanide (8,500 μg per kg), showing it's more poisonous orally. Intravenously, it's even deadlier—only 8 μg per kg is needed to be lethal in mice.

card.title: In pufferfish and beyond
card.body: Tetrodotoxin is found mainly in the liver and gonads of pufferfish, globefish, and toadfish, as well as in blue-ringed octopuses, rough-skinned newts, and moon snails. It can also be present in some shellfish and is produced by bacteria like Pseudoalteromonas, Pseudomonas, and Vibrio through symbiotic relationships. Human exposure occurs when consuming improperly prepared fish organs.

card.body: Theobromine is found in chocolate, tea (Camellia sinensis), American hollies (yaupon and guayusa), and the kola nut. It is also present in cacao beans and appears as a white or colourless solid, though commercial samples may be yellowish.

card.title: Official signal word: Warning
card.body: Vanillin carries the official GHS signal word "Warning". Its hazard statements: harmful if swallowed, and toxic to aquatic life with long lasting effects.

card.title: From Mesoamerica to synthetic labs
card.body: Vanilla beans were first used by the Totonacs in modern-day Veracruz, Mexico, as a flavoring for beverages around the early 15th century. The Aztecs used vanilla in chocolate drinks called xocohotl. In 1858, Théodore Nicolas Gobley isolated vanillin by evaporating vanilla extract and recrystallizing it. In 1874, Ferdinand Tiemann and Wilhelm Haarmann deduced its structure and developed a synthesis from coniferin, starting industrial production in Holzminden, Germany.

card.title: Scent of chocolate and ice cream
card.body: Vanillin is the primary component of vanilla bean extract and is widely used in sweet foods. It appears in ice cream and chocolate, which together make up 75% of vanillin's market. Synthetic vanillin is now more common than natural extract in foods, beverages, and pharmaceuticals.

card.title: Vanillin in 2nd millennium BCE jars
card.body: Vanillin residue was found in jars from a tomb in Canaan dating to the 2nd millennium BCE, suggesting vanilla cultivation may have occurred there long before the 16th century. This implies an unidentified Vanilla species could have been grown in the Old World since the Middle Bronze Age.
